questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Write short notes on meteorites.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Meaning and origin.** A **meteorite** is a **piece of rock or metal from space (a meteoroid) which survives its passage through the Earth's atmosphere and lands on the surface**. (While it is still falling and glowing it is a *meteor*, a "shooting star".) Most meteorites are **fragments of asteroids** from the **asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter**, which are left-over bodies of the early solar system; a very small number come from the **Moon and Mars**. They enter at high speed, and friction heats the outer surface, which melts to a thin dark **fusion crust**; some break up or leave **impact craters** (for example the Barringer crater in Arizona).

**Types.**

1. **Stony meteorites** (about 94 per cent of falls): made of silicate minerals (olivine, pyroxene) like the Earth's mantle. **Chondrites** contain small spherical grains called **chondrules** and are the most primitive (**carbonaceous chondrites** also hold carbon compounds and water); **achondrites** have no chondrules and are igneous rocks.
2. **Iron meteorites** (about 5 per cent): an **iron-nickel alloy** (kamacite and taenite) which shows the **Widmanstätten pattern** when polished and etched. They are thought to come from the **metallic cores** of broken planetesimals.
3. **Stony-iron meteorites** (about 1 per cent): a mixture of silicates and metal (pallasites, mesosiderites); the pallasites probably come from the **core-mantle boundary** of broken differentiated bodies.

**Importance.** Meteorites are the **oldest known solid material** and give, by **radiometric dating (lead-lead method), the age of the Earth and the solar system, about 4.56 billion years**; their composition shows **what the solar system was made from**; and iron meteorites and stony meteorites are used as **models of the Earth's core and mantle**, which cannot be sampled.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Outline the properties of body waves.

(6 marks)

(ii) State the various ways by which earthquakes can be predicted.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Properties of body waves.** Body waves are the seismic waves which **travel through the interior of the Earth** (as opposed to the surface waves, Love and Rayleigh). They are of two types.

**P-waves (primary, compressional or longitudinal waves).**

- The **particles move backwards and forwards parallel to the direction of travel** of the wave, so that the rock is alternately **compressed and stretched**, like a sound wave or a pushed spring.
- They are the **fastest** waves (about 5 to 7 km/s in the crust, about 8 km/s in the upper mantle and about 13 km/s in the lower mantle), so they are the **first to arrive** at a seismograph.
- They **pass through solids, liquids and gases**, so they travel through the **outer (liquid) core**, where they are **slowed and refracted**, which creates the **P-wave shadow zone** at about $103^\circ$ to $142^\circ$ from the focus.
- They have a smaller amplitude and cause less damage than the S-waves.

**S-waves (secondary or shear waves).**

- The **particles move at right angles (up and down or side to side) to the direction of travel**, so the rock is **sheared** (a "shake"), like a rope shaken.
- They are **slower** (about 60 per cent of the speed of P-waves, so about 3.5 km/s in the crust) and arrive **second**.
- They **pass only through solids**, since a liquid has no rigidity and cannot be sheared: **they are stopped by the liquid outer core**, which causes the **S-wave shadow zone** (all places farther than about $103^\circ$ from the focus), and is the evidence that the outer core is liquid.
- They have a **larger amplitude** and are more destructive.

**General properties of both.** Their velocity depends on the **density, rigidity and incompressibility of the material** ($V_P=\sqrt{\dfrac{K+\frac{4}{3}\mu}{\rho}}$ and $V_S=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mu}{\rho}}$, where $K$ is the bulk modulus, $\mu$ the rigidity and $\rho$ the density), and **generally increases with depth** because the rock is stiffer. They are **reflected and refracted at boundaries (the Moho, the Gutenberg discontinuity)** where the velocity changes suddenly, so their paths are **curved**, and a P-wave may be converted to an S-wave and the reverse at a boundary. These changes are used to **map the internal structure of the Earth**.

**(ii) Ways of predicting earthquakes.** An exact, short-term prediction is still not possible; the following methods are used to give **probable forecasts**:

1. **Past records and the seismic gap method:** the **frequency and recurrence interval of earlier earthquakes** along a fault, and a "seismic gap", a segment of an active fault which has not had an earthquake for a long time and is likely to be the next to break.
2. **Foreshocks and changes in microseismic activity** (a swarm of small tremors) before the main shock.
3. **Ground deformation:** **tilting, uplift or subsidence, and strain build-up** measured with tiltmeters, strain meters, laser distance measurement and **GPS or satellite radar** along the fault.
4. **Changes in underground water and gases:** a **rise or fall in the water level of wells, changes in water chemistry and temperature, and increased emission of radon gas**.
5. **Changes in the seismic wave velocities** (the P/S velocity ratio falls) and in the **electrical resistivity and magnetic field** of the rock before the shock.
6. **Unusual animal behaviour** (dogs, snakes and fish are said to be restless), which is not reliable.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) With respect to metamorphic rocks, define the term foliation.

(2 marks)

(ii) Account for the formation of foliation in rocks.

(2 marks)

(iii) List two non-foliated metamorphic rocks, stating their conditions of metamorphism, mineralogy and protolith.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Foliation.** Foliation is the **planar fabric of a metamorphic rock** produced by the **parallel (preferred) alignment of platy or elongate minerals** (micas, chlorite, hornblende) and/or **mineral banding**, which gives the rock a **tendency to split into thin layers along parallel surfaces**. The forms, in order of increasing grade, are **slaty cleavage, phyllitic sheen, schistosity and gneissic banding**.

**(ii) Formation of foliation.** Foliation forms when rock is subjected to **directed pressure (differential stress)**, as in **regional metamorphism at collision zones**. Under this stress, the **platy and elongate minerals recrystallise or grow, and existing grains are rotated, with their long (flat) faces perpendicular to the direction of maximum compression**; the grains are flattened by **pressure solution** and the minerals separate into light and dark bands at high grade. Where the pressure is equal in all directions (**confining pressure** only, or heat only), the minerals grow at random and no foliation develops.

**(iii) Two non-foliated metamorphic rocks.**

| | **Marble** | **Quartzite** |
|---|---|---|
| **Protolith** | limestone (or dolostone) | quartz sandstone (quartz arenite) |
| **Conditions of metamorphism** | **contact metamorphism** (around an igneous intrusion, high temperature and low pressure) or **regional metamorphism**; temperatures of several hundred degrees Celsius; **no directed pressure** is needed for the texture | **regional metamorphism** (burial and heating in orogenic belts, high temperature and pressure) or contact metamorphism |
| **Mineralogy** | **calcite** (or dolomite) in an **interlocking mosaic of equal-sized crystals** (granoblastic texture); impurities give wollastonite, garnet, etc. | almost entirely **quartz** (recrystallised **interlocking grains**, so the rock breaks across the grains) |
| **Texture** | granoblastic, sugary, no layering | granoblastic, very hard, no layering |

The protolith consists of **one mineral which does not form platy minerals**, which is why no foliation develops even under directed pressure. (Other non-foliated rocks: hornfels from shale or basalt by contact metamorphism, and anthracite from coal.)
